clue.text: Take by surprise and apprehend girl with goods

blocks.note: to apprehend a suspect is to catch them
a girl's name
goods for sale are wares; 'with' adds them on

explanation.surface: A police officer pounces on a woman carrying stolen merchandise, catching her off guard.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the front; everything after 'and' builds the phrase piece by piece.
explanation.definitionFit: To catch someone unawares is to come upon them when they least expect it, an idiom for surprising them.

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the noun: one used to refraining

blocks.note: AB, able seaman, is the usual crossword sailor
Sir John Stainer, Victorian composer of The Crucifixion

explanation.surface: A seafaring musician has grown accustomed to holding back from something.
explanation.walkthrough: Stainer is best known for church music, notably The Crucifixion; the hyphen in Sailor-composer just glues the two pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: An abstainer is a person who habitually goes without something, typically alcohol, so is accustomed to holding back.

clue.text: Church having the edge in lawbreaking

indicators.note: the church is said to have something within it, holding it inside

blocks.note: Church of England, abbreviated
a rim is an edge

explanation.surface: The church claims a moral advantage when it comes to wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Having the edge' reads as an idiom for being ahead; here the edge is a word placed inside the church abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: Crime is the general term for illegal acts, so it matches breaking the law as an abstract noun.

blocks.note: first meaning: honest, morally sound
second meaning: a vertical support or pole

explanation.walkthrough: 'Just a post' sounds like 'merely a post'; 'Just' is in fact the adjective meaning fair.
explanation.definitionFit: An honest, principled person is described as morally straight, and a vertical beam or goalpost is called by the same word.

blocks.note: first meaning: a formal talk given to an audience
second meaning: bearing or manner, an older sense of the word

explanation.surface: A lecture about how to carry oneself, as at a finishing school.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal oration is one sense; the other is a dated sense meaning poise, skill and bearing in handling oneself.

clue.text: A soldier-comedian getting on with stirring up public feeling

blocks.note: taken as written
GI is an American soldier
Jacques Tati, French film comedian of Monsieur Hulot
taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier and a comic star get along while whipping up popular unrest.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitation is a campaign to rouse people over a cause, so it is the act of arousing popular feeling.

indicators.note: something arising from words comes out of them, so the letters sit inside the phrase

blocks.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: A hidden irritation is causing someone's discontent.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is listless weariness and boredom, a jaded discontent with one's circumstances.

blocks.note: first meaning: a settlement reached by give and take
second meaning: lodgings, a place to stay

explanation.walkthrough: 'Compromise quarters' looks like an instruction to endanger someone's lodgings; it is two separate nouns.
explanation.definitionFit: Reaching an accommodation means settling a dispute by mutual concession, and the same word names housing or rooms provided for living.

blocks.note: scarlet is a bright red
a runner is a track athlete

explanation.surface: A communist sportsman turns out to be able to grow crops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red athlete' suggests a communist competitor; the colour and the athlete simply join.
explanation.definitionFit: The scarlet runner is a climbing bean with red flowers, grown in British gardens for its edible pods.

clue.text: Creed one has abandoned when ignominiously discharged

indicators.note: abandoned in the sense of wild and unrestrained, so the letters run loose

blocks.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who gave up their faith was thrown out in disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandoned' seems to say the creed was renounced; it is the signal to scramble the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To cashier an officer is to dismiss them from the armed forces in disgrace, a dishonourable dismissal.

blocks.note: first meaning: relating to or made of ions
second meaning: a classical metrical foot or metre

explanation.walkthrough: 'Electrically charged' suggests thrilling poetry, but chemistry and classical prosody each supply one meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Charged atoms are ions, giving the chemical adjective; in Greek and Latin prosody, Ionic metre is a recognised rhythm.

indicators.note: a selection is a portion picked out, here a run of consecutive letters

blocks.note: the run spans all three words

explanation.surface: A captain makes a speech on behalf of the side when the line-up is chosen.
explanation.definitionFit: To orate is to deliver a formal speech, often pompously, a grand word for talking.

clue.text: Soldier could be in danger? That's right!

indicators.note: what the word could be is another arrangement of its letters

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
i.e., id est, means 'that is'
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a soldier might be at risk, and is told yes, correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's right!' reads as agreement, but splits into the abbreviation i.e. and the letter for right.
explanation.definitionFit: A grenadier is an infantry soldier, originally one who threw grenades, now a member of the Grenadier Guards.

indicators.note: out in the sense of wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A wry question about a clock tower whose hours have expired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'time ran out' reads as a single idiom; the last word is the signal to rearrange the first two.
explanation.definitionFit: A minaret is the slender tall spire of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is made.

clue.text: Make fresh dispositions in back row

blocks.note: the rear is the back
a range, as of mountains, is a row

explanation.surface: A commander reorganises the troops standing in the back line.
explanation.definitionFit: Dispositions are arrangements of things or forces, so making new ones is to put them in a different order.

blocks.note: first meaning: a short tapered haircut fashionable in the 1920s
second meaning: the pebbles covering a seashore

explanation.surface: A query about which haircut suits a day at the seaside.
explanation.definitionFit: A shingle bob was a cropped 1920s women's cut; the same word means beach pebbles or a pebbly shore.

clue.text: Bird just right for old Michaelmas market

blocks.note: a goose is a bird
fair means just and equitable, right

explanation.surface: A goose is the ideal bird to buy at an autumn market; goose is the traditional Michaelmas dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Michaelmas is the feast of St Michael on 29 September. Nottingham's Goose Fair is an old fair traditionally held around then.
explanation.definitionFit: Nottingham's Goose Fair began as a market where geese were sold around Michaelmas, the late September church feast.

clue.text: Torpid party worker entered the Marines

indicators.note: the marines go into the gap between the party and the worker, entering them

blocks.note: a do is a party
RM, Royal Marines
the worker ant is the crossword's standard worker

explanation.surface: A sluggish political activist has joined the armed forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'party worker' looks like one political activist; it is two pieces with the marines entering between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Dormant means inactive, asleep or sluggish, as torpid animals in hibernation are.

clue.text: Flap over extraordinary rate for silk

indicators.note: something extraordinary is out of its normal order, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: a tab is a small flap
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone is in a panic about the excessive price charged for silk.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' places the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabaret is a striped upholstery fabric of silk with satin stripes, so a kind of silk material.

blocks.note: Con, short for Constance or Connie, as a girl's name
a tour is a round of visits

explanation.surface: A girl with a curvy figure.
explanation.walkthrough: Con is a pet form of Constance; the surface's curvy figure is itself a hint at the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A contour is the line marking the edge or shape of something, its profile or silhouette.

blocks.note: first meaning: a toady, someone who creeps to superiors
second meaning: the treecreeper, a small bird that climbs tree trunks

explanation.walkthrough: 'type of bird' suggests a species; 'type' belongs with 'Obsequious' instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A fawning sycophant is said to creep, making them one who crawls; the treecreeper family of small birds shares the name.

clue.text: Bloater paste at the French fair

indicators.note: paste is something mashed up, so the letters are pounded into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
le is French for the

explanation.surface: Fish spread is on sale at a French fete.
explanation.walkthrough: Bloater paste is a real British sandwich spread made from smoked herring; 'fair' looks like the funfair but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerable means acceptable but not outstanding, middling, which is one sense of the adjective fair.

blocks.note: first meaning: not heavy
second meaning: a source of illumination

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a handy camping lamp; it is two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that weighs little is easy to carry, and a lamp is one example of an illuminating fitting.

blocks.note: S, south, is a point of the compass
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: Someone gestures towards the rear of a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The stern is the rear part of a ship, and so by extension the back of anything.

clue.text: Spaniards used round ring as a net

indicators.note: the word is used turned about, taken in the opposite direction
goes round means surrounds the following piece

blocks.note: Spanish gentlemen are dons
a ring has the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: Spanish men employed a hoop as a mesh.
explanation.walkthrough: Don is a Spanish title for a gentleman, so Spaniards are dons; turned about, they wrap round the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A snood is a hairnet or ornamental mesh bag worn at the back of a woman's head.

blocks.note: first meaning: a publication serving as a mouthpiece
second meaning: the keyboard instrument with pipes

explanation.surface: A rolled-up paper is pressed into service as a makeshift instrument, like a comb and paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A periodical voicing an organisation's views is its official mouthpiece; the church keyboard with pipes shares the same name.

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
probate is the legal proving of a will

explanation.surface: A legal objection about the proof offered for a will.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Censure' is the verb here: to reprobate is to condemn strongly.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to reprobate means to express strong disapproval of, to condemn or rebuke.

clue.text: Barrow boys way ahead of Red Star characters

indicators.note: the words are treated as a set of letters, characters free to be laid out again

blocks.note: a street is a way
the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Market vendors are well in front of a team of communist celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: Barrow boys are British market traders selling from handcarts; Red Star suggests a Soviet emblem or a sports club.
explanation.definitionFit: A barrow boy sells goods from a cart in the street, so the plural is vendors who sell outdoors.
